etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stert, from the verb sterten (“to start, startle”). See below.

definitions.definition: The beginning of an activity.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:
quote.text: I see you stand like greyhounds in the slips, / Straining upon the start.

definitions.definition: A sudden involuntary movement.

quote.citation: 1692, Roger L’Estrange, “ (please specify the fable number.) (please specify the name of the fable.)”, in Fables, of Æsop and Other Eminent Mythologists: […], London:  […]  R[ichard] Sare, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: Nature does nothing by starts and leaps, or in a hurry.

quote.citation: 1885, Robert Louis Stevenson, Olalla:
quote.text: The sight of his scared face, his starts and pallors and sudden harkenings, unstrung me  […]

definitions.definition: The beginning point of a race, a board game, etc.
An appearance in a sports game, horserace, etc., from the beginning of the event.

quote.citation: 2011 February 12, Ian Hughes, “Arsenal 2 - 0 Wolverhampton”, in BBC‎[1]:
quote.text: Wilshere, who made his first start for England in the midweek friendly win over Denmark, raced into the penalty area and chose to cross rather than shoot - one of the very few poor selections he made in the match.

definitions.definition: (horticulture) A young plant germinated in a pot to be transplanted later.

quote.citation: 2009, Liz Primeau, Steven A. Frowine, Gardening Basics For Canadians For Dummies:
quote.text: You generally see nursery starts at garden centres in mid to late spring. Small annual plants are generally sold in four-packs or larger packs, with each cell holding a single young plant.

definitions.definition: An initial advantage over somebody else; a head start.
(UK, slang, archaic) A happening or proceeding.

quote.citation: 1887, Hawley Smart, A False Start, volume 2, page 69:
quote.text: “It's a rum start, old John Madingley's coming down to Tunnleton,” said Grafton, one evening in the smoking-room;  […]

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English sterten (“to leap up suddenly, rush out”), from Old English styrtan (“to leap up, start”), from Proto-West Germanic *sturtijan (“to startle, move, set in motion”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ter- (“to be stiff”). Cognate with Old Frisian stirta (“to fall down, tumble”), Middle Dutch sterten (“to rush, fall, collapse”) (Dutch storten), Old High German sturzen (“to hurl, plunge, turn upside down”) (German stürzen), Old High German sterzan (“to be stiff, protrude”). More at stare.

definitions.definition: To set in motion.

quote.citation: April 2, 1716, Joseph Addison, Freeholder No. 30
quote.text: I was some years ago engaged in conversation with a fashionable French Abbe, upon a subject which the people of that kingdom love to start in discourse.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter XXII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: In the autumn there was a row at some cement works about the unskilled labour men. A union had just been started for them and all but a few joined. One of these blacklegs was laid for by a picket and knocked out of time.

definitions.definition: To begin.

quote.citation: 2013 July 19, Peter Wilby, “Finland spreads word on schools”, in The Guardian Weekly, volume 189, number 6, page 30:
quote.text: Imagine a country where children do nothing but play until they start compulsory schooling at age seven. Then, without exception, they attend comprehensives until the age of 16. Charging school fees is illegal, and so is sorting pupils into ability groups by streaming or setting.

definitions.definition: To ready the operation of a vehicle or machine.
To put or raise (a question, an objection); to put forward (a subject for discussion).
To bring onto being or into view; to originate; to invent.

quote.citation: 1674, William Temple, letter to The Countess of Essex:
quote.text: Sensual men agree in the pursuit of every pleasure they can start.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To begin, commence, initiate.
(intransitive) To begin an activity.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: Thinks I to myself, “Sol, you're run off your course again. This is a rich man's summer ‘cottage’  […] .” So I started to back away again into the bushes. But I hadn't backed more'n a couple of yards when I see something so amazing that I couldn't help scooching down behind the bayberries and looking at it.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To have its origin (at), begin.
(intransitive) To jerk suddenly in surprise.

quote.citation: c. 1597 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merry Wiues of Windsor”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene v]:
quote.text: But if he start,  It is the flesh of a corrupted heart.

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene v], page 257, column 2:
quote.text: I could a Tale vnfold, vvhoſe lighteſt vvord  VVould harrovv vp thy ſoule, freeze thy young blood,  Make thy tvvo eyes like Starres, ſtart from their Spheres,  Thy knotty and combined locks to part,  And each particular haire to ſtand an end,  Like Quilles vpon the fretfull Porpentine:  […]

quote.citation: 1681, John Dryden, The Spanish Fryar: Or, the Double Discovery. […], London:  […]  Richard Tonson and Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC, (please specify the page number):
quote.text: I start as from some dreadful dream.

quote.citation: 1725, Isaac Watts, Logick: Or, The Right Use of Reason in the Enquiry after Truth, […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  John Clark and Richard Hett, […], Emanuel Matthews, […], and Richard Ford, […], published 1726, →OCLC:
quote.text: Keep your soul to the work when it is ready to start aside.

quote.citation: 1855, Robert Browning, Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came, section XXXI:
quote.text: [...] The tempest's mocking elf  Points to the shipman thus the unseen shelf  He strikes on, only when the timbers start.

quote.citation: 1891, Oscar Wilde, chapter VIII, in The Picture of Dorian Gray, London, New York, N.Y., Melbourne, Vic.: Ward Lock & Co., →OCLC, page 139:
quote.text: Suddenly his eye fell on the screen that he had placed in front of the portrait, and he started.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To awaken suddenly.

quote.citation: 1816 June – 1817 April/May (date written), [Mary Shelley], chapter IV, in Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. […], volume I, London:  […]  [Macdonald and Son] for Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor, & Jones, published 1 January 1818, →OCLC, page 100:
quote.text: I started from my sleep with horror; a cold dew covered my forehead, my teeth chattered, and every limb became convulsed; [...]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To disturb and cause to move suddenly; to startle; to alarm; to rouse; to cause to flee or fly.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:
quote.text: Upon malicious bravery dost thou come  To start my quiet?

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To flinch or draw back.

quote.citation: 1836, Elizur Wright, Quarterly Anti-slavery Magazine, volume 2, page 162:
quote.text: Physical poison would make them start from arsenicked bread; shall not the moral poison which is in it, make them start more promptly still from slave produce?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To move suddenly from its place or position; to displace or loosen; to dislocate.

quote.citation: 1676, Richard Wiseman, Severall Chirurgicall Treatises, London:  […]  E. Flesher and J. Macock, for R[ichard] Royston […], and B[enjamin] Took, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: One, by a fall in wrestling, started the end of the clavicle from the sternon.

definitions.definition: To startle or be startled; to move or be moved suddenly.
(intransitive) To break away, to come loose.

quote.citation: 1749, [John Cleland], “[Letter the First]”, in Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure [Fanny Hill], volume I, London:  […]  [Thomas Parker] for G. Fenton [i.e., Fenton and Ralph Griffiths] […], →OCLC, page 76:
quote.text: [...] we could, with the greateſt eaſe, as well as clearneſs, ſee all objects, (ourſelves unſeen) only by applying our eyes cloſe to the crevice, where the moulding of a pannel had warp'd, or ſtarted a little on the other ſide.

definitions.definition: (transitive, sports) To put into play.

quote.citation: 2010, Brian Glanville, The Story of the World Cup: The Essential Companion to South Africa 2010, London: Faber and Faber, →ISBN, page 361:
quote.text: The charge against Zagallo then is not so much that he started Ronaldo, but that when it should surely have been clear that the player was in no fit state to take part he kept him on.

quote.citation: 2024 May 6, Sid Lowe, “Portu’s brilliant burst seals Girona’s top-four fairytale in the perfect way”, in The Guardian‎[2], →ISSN:
quote.text: “Look at Portu,” Michel insisted, “he scores goals and I never start him. He says: ‘You’re sinking me, but OK, I’ll just go out and score again.’”

definitions.definition: (transitive, nautical) To pour out; to empty; to tap and begin drawing from.
(intransitive, euphemistic) To start one's periods (menstruation).
An instance of starting.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English stert, start (“tail, handle, projection”), from Old English steort, from Proto-West Germanic *stert, from Proto-Germanic *stertaz (“tail”). Cognate with Scots start, stairt (“side-post, shaft, upright post”), Dutch staart (“tail”), German Sterz (“tail, handle”), Swedish stjärt (“tail, arse”).

definitions.definition: A projection or protrusion; that which pokes out.
A handle, especially that of a plough.
The curved or inclined front and bottom of a water wheel bucket.

quote.citation: 1845, Captain R.E. Crawley, Description of a Water-Course, Wharf, and Water-Wheel, erected at Waltham Abbey, Essex […] :
quote.text: The fall of water is 6 feet, and the radius of the curve is 8 feet, from the centre of the water-wheel to the extreme point of the start.

definitions.definition: The arm, or level, of a gin, drawn around by a horse.
(dialectal, archaic) Completely, utterly.

quote.citation: 1828 August 22, “Militia System”, in The New England Farmer, volume VII, Boston, M.A.: John B. Russell, published 1829, page 40, column 1:
quote.text: Col.—The age has no sense—the people are start mad—as mad as a March mare. We should have fine times, indeed if our laws did'nt compel the poor people to protect the property of the rich.
